title: Don’t panic over your fragile QBs, Falcons fans. Focus on Bijan Robinson and Drake London Atlanta has bona fide stars, but its success might hinge on the unstable and anxiety-inducing pair of Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr. Candace Buckner

full_text:
Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa recovers his own fumble against the Broncos during last week's preseason game in Atlanta. Kevin C. Cox / Getty Images
WESTFIELD, Ind. — Woosah , Atlanta Falcons fans. There are plenty of reasons on your roster to keep you calm and steady this season.
Starting, of course, with Bijan Robinson, the all-purpose player who helped elevate the status of running backs in the league — in real life and in the fantasy world. On Wednesday afternoon, just before the Falcons’ joint practice with the Indianapolis Colts, a young boy in blue rushed over to the enemy’s side and screamed: “ Bee-jaann! Bee-jaaan ! I have you on my fantasy team! Do good this season!”
Robinson nicely played along, smiled and gave him a thumbs-up.
Then, there’s Drake London, the high-flyer in football pads, who created two of the best highlights from Wednesday’s practice with his velcro hands and trampoline legs.
So, breathe. It’ll be all right … long as you don’t pay too much attention to the men tasked with handing the ball off to Robinson, or lobbing it deep to London.
This is where the panic kicks in, and the stress sweats every Sunday afternoon, and the public prayers at the altar of Arch. Because with Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr., the Falcons have the most anxiety-inducing quarterback room in the NFL.
Not quite as dysfunctional as the Cleveland Browns; that depth chart of Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders just might launch more train-wreck headlines this season than actual completions on the field. However, the Falcons’ QB room must overcome a more troubling quality: fragility.
First, consider Tagovailoa, who’s in the pole position for QB1. He has experienced at least four documented head injuries that span from his college days into his time as the Miami Dolphins’ franchise quarterback. Scratch that — former franchise quarterback.
His last concussion in 2024, after he had signed a four-year, $212.4 million contract extension, Tagovailoa collided with Damar Hamlin, as slight as can be when it comes to defensive backs in the league, and displayed an unnatural and frightening fencing position with his hands and arms. The concussion caused him to miss four weeks. When he returned later that season, he threw 17 interceptions through his final nine games. Last year, the Dolphins benched Tagovailoa, then released him in March, deciding to take a record $99 million hit against the salary cap rather than stick with him.
Now in his reboot with the Falcons, and while trying to develop a connection with his receivers, he just doesn’t look like the same Tua .
Also, there’s this fact: Tagovailoa is only taking first-team reps because he’s faced no competition yet. Three weeks into training camp, and Penix hasn’t been medically cleared for contact, nor is he mentally ready to return to the game.
Penix, the backup who was taken as the fourth quarterback in the 2024 NFL Draft, has endured three ACL tears that began during his time in college and into his development as the Falcons’ franchise quarterback. Correction — potential franchise quarterback.
His most recent ACL injury, in his left knee, occurred last November. By that time, he had been benched during a Week 3 blowout loss to Carolina and had endured a three-game losing streak before another debilitating tear ended his second season.
Now in the critical third year of his NFL career, and while already behind due to his inability to take part in 11-on-11 work, Penix hasn’t shown that he can be the quarterback the franchise thought when it used a first-round pick on him. Mostly, because of this: “Physically, I’ve got a good ACL. I can go out there and do anything. But mentally, I hesitate. It’s like, ‘Do I trust it?’” Penix confessed recently on Cam Newton’s podcast.
Between this pair of lefty quarterbacks — one who’ll make you cringe every time his head hits the ground, and the other who’ll make you flinch any time he reaches for his knee — the Falcons have recklessly constructed their depth chart. The franchise has done little to inspire confidence in the most important position on the field, adding to the angst that has existed at QB for years, going back to the post-Matt Ryan era. The Falcons might be two plays away from having to rely on career backup Cooper Rush all season. And new head coach Kevin Stefanski thought he had escaped chaos when he left Cleveland.
There’s nothing wrong with Tagovailoa, the teammate. In Westfield, he roamed the sideline, searching for helmets and hands to smack. When Penix zipped a short completion in 7-on-7s — the only action Penix has seen through training camp because even in a red jersey, he can’t risk being touched — Tagovailoa called out: “Nice, Mike!” For Tagovailoa, communication is everything.
“I would say after a play, I just go up to the guys and talk to them, like: ‘Hey, talk to me. What did you think on that? What are you feeling?’” Tagovailoa said about building a connection with his receivers. “‘Did you like it? Did you not like it?’ Things like that. And then their level of comfort with the play, if they don’t feel comfortable running that back, I don’t want to waste my time trying to time that up with them, if they don’t feel comfortable with that.”
Still, as much as Tagovailoa is trying as a teammate, his early performances as Atlanta’s QB1 have been shaky. Tua never particularly had a big arm, and now he does not, or cannot, consistently throw the ball downfield.
During the Falcons’ Aug. 14 preseason opener against the Denver Broncos, he attempted five passes, with none traveling farther than 5 yards in the air. Then on Wednesday, a jump ball to London notwithstanding, this trend continued during his play against the Colts’ first-team defense. In the teams’ final 11-on-11 action, Tua’s first pass fell incomplete. His second, a short one intended for London, landed in the hands of Colts cornerback Justin Walley and would’ve accounted for a pick-six in a real game. Overall, Tagovailoa had an up-and-down practice , fumbling a snap and often feeling a wall of blue in the pocket. On Sundays, those would’ve been sacks, and grounds for Falcons fans to freak out.
So, Atlanta, try to look away from Tagovailoa’s short game and ignore Penix’s distrust of his body. Instead, focus on Robinson bouncing out of the backfield and the 6-foot-4 London springing over most defenders to make a catch. (London spoke so confidently about his abilities on Wednesday that he joked with Falcons beat reporter D. Orlando Ledbetter that even if the journalist were his quarterback, he’d still haul in passes.)
Maybe all that skill might keep you sane. Even if dread exists in that quarterback room.

full_text:
Falcons quarterback Michael Penix has still not been cleared for 11-on-11 work in practice. Justin Casterline / Getty Images
WESTFIELD, Ind. — Kevin Stefanski was encouraged by the progress his Atlanta Falcons made in two days of joint practices against the Indianapolis Colts here this week, but the most critical question of training camp moved no closer to a resolution. And the Falcons still don’t have a timetable for naming a starting quarterback, Stefanski said Thursday.
“We will cross that bridge when we get there,” he said. “Like I see with every other battle on the roster, guys are working hard.”
That will be an understandably unsatisfactory answer for many fans, but there are still too many questions the coaches can’t answer. Tua Tagovailoa did little over the course of two days to separate himself from Michael Penix Jr., who still is being held out of 11-on-11 work by the surgeon who repaired the torn ACL that ended his 2025 season in Week 11. Penix had a meeting scheduled with his doctor on Thursday evening.
“As far as moving in the pocket, I can do everything,” Penix said. “If I had a rush coming at me, I can get away. It’s just, if I don’t get away, that’s what we’re thinking about right now — if I don’t get away. I don’t think my doctor is ready for me to take those hits right now, but that time is coming real soon.”
Penix wants to fully return to practice but will not lobby his doctor to release him, he said.
“I mean, I would never argue with a doctor,” he said. “I feel like they know more than me as far as the body. I’m just going to trust what he says and trust God and, like I always say, continue to run my race. Whatever he says, that’s what it’s going to be, and I’m going to trust him and trust God and keep taking steps in the right direction.”
Penix had surgery on Nov. 25 last year and said at the end of July he was probably four weeks from being cleared. The Falcons and Colts will play a preseason game on Saturday at Lucas Oil Stadium, but Atlanta’s starters will not see any action. If Penix is cleared by his doctor this week, the earliest he could get on the field is Monday’s practice.
“He’s doing a great job,” Stefanski said. “He’s preparing as if he’s getting every rep out here.”
Penix was 2-for-5 passing with an interception in seven-on-seven work against the Colts on Thursday. His last pass was an interception in a red zone drill.
“I want to take advantage of every rep that I get, but today I ended on a bad play, so now I have to sit there thinking about that was my last play,” he said.
Meanwhile, Tagovailoa was 7-of-14 with three touchdowns in 11-on-11 work in the red zone. He was 1-of-3 in seven-on-seven drills. Tagovailoa started well in a two-minute drill late in practice, completing two passes to Drake London and one to Bijan Robinson to move Atlanta to midfield but then threw four straight incompletions to end the day. In Wednesday and Thursday’s practices combined, he was 15-of-27.
Stefanski called Tagovailoa’s practice on Thursday “good,” putting most of the issues on poor pass blocking.
“I think our protection needs to clean up in a lot of areas, and the quarterback plays a role in that as well,” the coach said.
Here are some additional takeaways from Thursday’s action:
Za’Darius Smith will bring a veteran presence and lots of energy to Atlanta’s edge rusher room, Stefanski said.
“Big personality, you are going to hear him before you see him,” Stefanski said. “He has heavy hands, excellent against the run, was an excellent teammate for us.”
Smith played for Stefanski in Cleveland in 2023 and the first half of 2024 before being traded. Smith, who has 70.5 sacks in an 11-year NFL career, briefly retired at the end of the 2025 season but decided to return this offseason and signed a one-year deal with the Falcons earlier this week. He did not participate in either joint practice and will not play in Saturday’s game.
“I have a comfort level with Za’Darius the person and Za’Darius the player,” Stefanski said.
Bijan Robinson is keeping score on the highlights the Falcons post on social media.
“I know they don’t show too much run stuff on social media, but I feel like we did very well hat-on-hat and showing a glimpse of what we are going to be this season,” Robinson said after Thursday’s practice. “I thought we did very well.”
Robinson got a lot of work over the two days, although no running backs were tackled to the ground.
“I always love to compete against other guys. It’s always fun,” he said. “You can’t walk out there and not bring intensity.”
Third-string running back Tyler Goodson left Thursday’s practice after a collision with a Colts linebacker during a blocking drill. Goodson did not return but remained on the sideline.
Tight end Kyle Pitts playfully declined to discuss how much time the Falcons have spent practicing their screen game so far, which only strengthens my belief that it’s going to be a big part of the offense.
“That’s a schematic question. I can’t give you that answer,” Pitts said with a grin.
It’s tough not to see this as a bad week for undrafted free agent quarterback Jack Strand. The feel-good story of the first week of training camp did not take a snap in any team work against the Colts, but Stefanski said he will play half of Saturday’s preseason game.
Veteran Cooper Rush took all the second-team snaps in 11-on-11 drills and looks to have officially taken over the No. 3 quarterback position.
Jawaan Taylor’s return to the right tackle spot made a noticeable difference for the Falcons on Wednesday and Thursday. Taylor missed the first two weeks of training camp rehabbing a knee injury.
“Good to get Jawaan going,” Stefanski said. “I thought there were some really good moments out there, pleased with where he is.”
Left tackle Jack Matthews is still dealing with a minor injury but did more 11-on-11 work Thursday than Wednesday, when he had only one series. Michael Jerrell took a step forward in the battle for the swing tackle position, working at right and left tackle on Thursday, while Wanya Morris didn’t take any team reps.
• The Falcons showed London’s leaping touchdown catch on Wednesday during their team meeting Thursday morning, Stefanski said. “Yeah, pretty good catch,” the coach deadpanned. “He can do many things, and one of the things he can do is elevate to go get the football. His body control is elite.”
• Wide receiver Chris Blair took the snaps Jahan Dotson usually gets with the first-team offense during red zone work Thursday.
• Safety Jessie Bates participated in pre-practice drills but got no team work.
• Defensive tackle LaCale London returned to team drills.

title: Dalton Kincaid shines, Skyler Bell’s status and more Bills-Browns practice takeaways The Bills and Browns wrapped up their joint practice on Thursday with an eye toward Saturday's preseason game. Joe Buscaglia

full_text:
Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen is unsure he will play in Saturday's preseason game against the Browns. David Richard / Associated Press
BEREA, Ohio — For the third year in a row, the Buffalo Bills made it part of their preseason plan to hit the road early and partake in a joint practice with their upcoming exhibition opponents. After heading to Pittsburgh in 2024 and Chicago in 2025, the Bills went to the Cleveland Browns’ practice home to take on an eager group looking to measure their progress against the Bills, a perennial Super Bowl contender.
The allure of joint practices for NFL teams is a pretty easy sell. Although it raises the risk of a more intense practice than they would have if the Bills stayed in Orchard Park, it gives both teams a chance to call their real offenses and defenses without the entire NFL world seeing it, and to control the contact as best they can to protect their players. In preseason games, teams generally don’t use their full playbooks and every play is live.
The other piece of joint practices, for an expected playoff team like the Bills, is that it may give them all the work they want against an opponent while resting their most important players for the upcoming preseason game. When Bills head coach Joe Brady was asked if that was his plan, he certainly left the door open to sitting his stars Saturday against the Browns.
Most of the talk about who plays Saturday revolves around star quarterback Josh Allen.
Although production wasn’t the top draw, the Bills’ first-team offense looked polished all day against a well-respected Browns defense. To no one’s surprise, Allen was the best player on the field as he ran six different sets of 11-on-11 team drills.
In Allen’s opinion, the energy from the offense and defense was high during the session, which could be a hint at how the Bills are leaning on Saturday. For reference, in the Bills’ last two joint practices in 2024 and 2025, Allen did not play in the following preseason game against the Steelers and Bears, though he played the middle when asked about playing Saturday.
“Whatever coach asks me to do,” Allen said. “Whether I play or not, I’m going to be happy with the decision.”
Here are four takeaways from what might have been their most important practice of the summer.
If you spend any part of your day scrolling through social media, odds are you saw the very open Dalton Kincaid rope on a 54-yard touchdown on the second play of their two-minute drill. No one was home for the Browns on the play, but it underscores his explosiveness and downfield potential in the Bills’ offense.
The last two seasons with him have been frustrating for him, the team, fans and fantasy football managers alike. The talent is obvious but injuries have weighed him down so much over the last two seasons that he’s missed nine regular-season games; even worse, his playing time dipped to 50 percent in games played in 2024 and 39 percent in games played in 2025. The injuries, plus his blocking concerns, made the Bills a highly predictable team when Kincaid was on the field, and they were very likely to throw the ball. All of it made some wonder if he’d ever be more than just an important bit player on a good offense.
However, this camp and preseason have looked and felt a bit different for Kincaid. He’s been at practice every day, he looks stronger and he’s playing with more physicality in the blocking game. Most importantly, his usage during camp practices has seen a bit of a bump — even with tight ends Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes fully healthy. It’s not to say that he’s on the precipice of playing 75 percent or more of the team’s offensive snaps, but Kincaid’s health, summer usage, and ability are all trending toward an enhanced role in 2026.
“It’s no secret that we’re a better offense when he’s on the field,” Allen said of Kincaid. “He opens up so much. He’s a tough matchup for linebackers, and I think he’s a tough matchup for cornerbacks, for that matter. He just continues to make plays and be elusive without the ball in his hands, and when he gets the ball in his hands, he just finds a way to keep moving forward.”
For tight ends who appeared in at least 14 games, Kincaid led the league with 2.73 yards per route run, having been targeted on 24 percent of all his routes. The next closest player was Chicago’s Colston Loveland at 1.98 yards per route run.
After the Bills’ preseason opener, Brady gave a somewhat encouraging update on rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell, saying they hoped to get him on the field for practice this week. The practice week is now over, and Bell didn’t get back the way they hoped. However, with the entire team on the other field, Bell snuck out of the locker room and began running drills in the distance with the strength and conditioning staff.
This was the first time we’ve seen Bell since he suffered what the Bills termed a “lower body injury.” After the practice concluded, The Athletic caught up with Bell, and he explained what he’s dealing with and where he is in his recovery.
Bell disclosed that he suffered a groin injury during the team’s first practice in Highmark Stadium on Aug. 8, and Thursday marked the first time he’s been spotted during a practice working with staff since.
“Man, it just felt good to get these pads on,” Bell said. “I actually wasn’t supposed to put them on, but since they said I was running a little bit fast, I wanted to get used to putting them back on.”
In addition to rehabbing the injury, the rookie receiver said a part of the rehabbing process was in the mental battle.
“I was super, super frustrated,” Bell said. “You dream all the time to be in this position, and you work so hard to get here, and it’s taken away from you. So you just try not to take things for granted. I was glad to be back out here running a little bit with the pads on, having my helmet on in here. So, it felt good.”
Bell admitted that he probably won’t play on Saturday against the Browns, but said his goal is to play in the team’s final preseason game against the Steelers on Aug. 27 if all goes well.
The Bills just welcomed projected starting cornerback Maxwell Hairston back to practice this Tuesday for the first time since he suffered a groin injury. Before the injury, Hairston was inconsistent in coverage throughout training camp, especially when he had to deal with a physical receiver.
Heading into the joint practices, I was especially interested in how he would fare against rookie wide receiver Denzel Boston, who by most accounts in Cleveland has been a standout performer. Boston is a physical, 6-foot-4, 215-pound receiver matching up against the much smaller Hairston. To Hairston’s credit, he broke up a pass to end the Browns’ two-minute drill after the Browns scrambled to get to the line and did a last-second heave to the end zone. The rest of the day was a clear and consistent win for Boston in the matchup. They targeted him successfully several times throughout the day, and even when they weren’t, Boston was winning the matchup. If it were a one-off, that’d be one thing, but dealing with physicality has been a consistent battle for Hairston all summer.
The Bills also haven’t brought back Hairston in full just yet. Before the injury, he was taking most of the initial first-team reps during team drills. Upon his return, there has been more mixing and matching of team drill reps, with rookie second-round pick Davison Igbinosun getting first-team time. That could be because they want to work Hairston back in slowly, but with Hairston’s struggles, the door is open for Igbinosun to fight for the starting role.
Either way — even with moonlighting boundary corner Dee Alford on the roster — the Bills need to weigh all options ahead of the regular season and decide soon if signing a veteran for insurance will help secure one of the biggest questions on their defense.

full_text:
Shedeur Sanders (right) will get the start in Saturday's preseason game against the Bills, with Deshaun Watson (left) expected to play in the third quarter. David Richard / Associated Press
BEREA, Ohio — Decision time is coming in the Cleveland Browns’ quarterback competition, but coach Todd Monken maintains he’s still evaluating — and that his plan for Saturday’s preseason game remains unchanged.
Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders split the reps with the No. 1 offense in Thursday’s joint practice with the Buffalo Bills. Watson was first up and started last weekend’s preseason opener . Sanders will start Saturday’s game versus Buffalo.
Sanders got the two-minute situation in Thursday’s joint session and moved the offense inside the Buffalo 15-yard line before a third-down sack essentially ended the Browns’ chances of matching the Bills’ score. On a day Monken said his team “looked like we belong” on the field against one of the NFL’s best, both quarterbacks had positive moments.
Watson had the day’s longest completions , both to speedy rookie KC Concepcion, but he also threw the only interception of the controlled practice. Sanders relied on Cleveland’s other rookie wide receiver, Denzel Boston, to twice move the chains in the two-minute drill and tried to hit Boston on a fade route as time expired. But Boston was well covered and unable to come down with the catch.
Thursday’s sharing of the work was part of Monken’s plan. After Watson played the first half Saturday in Chicago and then Sanders played the next three series, that will flip this weekend — though many of the starters for both teams won’t be on the field.
“I haven’t looked at the tape from today, and we haven’t played Saturday, so that’s all still part of (the evaluation),” Monken said. “Just like every day is.”
Watson and Sanders have alternated days with the No. 1 offense since the spring in every practice but one, a session almost two weeks ago in which Watson took all the No. 1 reps and performed well. The Browns’ only two scoring drives in the preseason opener came with Watson behind center, though both quarterbacks were up and down in that game and in the practice days that followed.
The joint practice loomed as both a key evaluation point and probably one of the last. Watson got the first six snaps Thursday in the first drill, while Sanders was first up in the seven-on-seven drill and the two-minute situation (1:50 on the clock, one timeout, needing a touchdown to win).
The Browns have held 18 training camp practices and have two next week ahead of their preseason finale Thursday versus the New England Patriots. Monken said this week that he’d like to have a starter in place already and, because he doesn’t, would like to be able to name one by Monday. But he hasn’t committed to that, leaving open the possibility Sanders could extend the competition if he performs well Saturday.
“We wanted to make sure we got them reps (Thursday),” Monken said. “But right in the middle of the (first team drill), you sub in the quarterback, and that’s not always easy. But screw it — spot the ball (and) make a damn play. That’s part of it, too.
“What we wanted to see today (was) do we belong? Does our first 11 give us a chance to move the ball and score? I felt that way today.”
Thursday was a needed change of environment. Things have been testy between the offense and defense in Browns camp, and by now the Cleveland defense has seen just about everything the offense wants to run regardless of who’s under center. Now comes a change in venue — and Watson’s first action at Huntington Bank Field since some fans cheered after he suffered a torn right Achilles tendon in October 2024.
Monken, who spent the last three seasons as the Baltimore Ravens’ offensive coordinator, wasn’t employed by the Browns for any of Watson’s 19 previous starts. Until last weekend, Monken rarely mentioned the past or any potential dynamics involved with a player and a franchise-altering trade that Browns owner Jimmy Haslam labeled “a swing and miss” in early 2025.
But Watson remains under contract for one more season because of the Browns’ salary-cap commitments to him. If Monken decides Watson gives these young Browns their best chance, the fanbase will expect Watson to do what he hasn’t done before: help the team win consistently.
It probably wasn’t a coincidence that in a close, shared competition with just one noticeable difference — Watson’s 73 games and seven seasons of NFL experience versus Sanders’ seven starts as a rookie — Monken chose to start Watson in the lone road preseason game and Sanders in the first home one.
The stadium might be only a quarter full Saturday by the time Watson takes the field, so it’s hard to say if the home crowd’s reaction toward him will be negative. Might he get booed?
“I don’t care,” Watson said Wednesday, repeating that he’s still focused on mastering the offense and finding his timing after last week marked his first game action in 22 months.
“Every situation, every rep I get, every opportunity I get to just go out there and play football is just as important as playing just one quarter or playing a lot in practice,” he added. “I think the more reps I get, the more opportunities I get to see, are more beneficial for myself and just improving my game and just catching up from what I missed the last two years.
“There’s always room to grow, even Week 1 to Week 17. … Every opportunity, every rep that we get standing back there in the pocket, is definitely an opportunity for us to get more comfortable.”
That’s even if it gets uncomfortable Saturday, or in a future game in Cleveland. And even if the competition has to continue beyond this weekend.

Campbell said he wants to play some of his starters. Jared Goff won’t play, but th
full_text:
Rookie Luke Altmyer has gotten a lot of second-team snaps and has an opportunity to force the Detroit coaches into a difficult decision. Sam Greene / Imagn Images
ALLEN PARK, Mich. — Another test awaits Dan Campbell’s Detroit Lions, as the team prepares for its second of three preseason games Saturday against the Washington Commanders at noon ET at Ford Field. With it comes another batch of players worth watching.
Campbell said he wants to play some of his starters. Jared Goff won’t play, but this will be a chance for some of the vets to shake off the rust in a gamelike atmosphere, especially since the Lions aren’t participating in joint practices this year. More importantly, though, it’ll be a chance to solidify roster spots and show continued growth.
Last week’s edition featured the likes of first-round pick Blake Miller, Ahmed Hassanein (two sacks and five pressures), Skyler Gill-Howard (three pressures), Nick Whiteside and Ennis Rakestraw, as well as center Seth McLaughlin. They’re worth continued monitoring, but we’ll use this opportunity to highlight others competing for roster spots.
When training camp began, Detroit’s QB room was largely settled. Teddy Bridgewater was the No. 2, and Altmyer’s best shot at sticking around was on the practice squad as a developmental QB.
How quickly things change. Bridgewater retired, Dobbs was added, and Altmyer earned the attention of Campbell and this coaching staff.
Even with a veteran such as Dobbs in the mix, Altmyer has been the first QB on the field when the Lions turn to their second-team offense — rather consistently. Part of that is because Dobbs is new to the offense and still learning the playbook. But part of it is because the Lions are trying to get Altmyer as many reps as possible. It seems as if they legitimately like what he brings to the table.
“Dobbs is a bright guy,” Campbell said. “He’s played in this league. But also, man, just making sure it got him up to speed, being true to that. And also Luke’s a young player, but he’s promising … trying to soak him with reps. So, it was just kind of a little bit of that, but we’ll get a look at Dobbs here and let him go.”
Campbell said Dobbs will start versus the Commanders, so perhaps he’s finally getting up to speed with the offense. His practice results have been a mixed bag, but he’s a smart veteran who fits the mold of what the Lions like behind Goff. That said, Altmyer has a chance to make this interesting and earn a spot as a third QB. Not something we typically see here, but it’s not out of the question.
We didn’t see Moore — Detroit’s second-round pick — in the opener. He was working his way back from a groin injury that forced him to miss a handful of practices.
Since returning and getting his feet under him, however, he’s been on an absolute heater.
The Lions have deployed Moore in a variety of ways, giving him (pun intended) more and more opportunities with the first-team defense. He’ll rush off the edge, he’ll kick inside to three-technique, he’ll run stunts and twists, he’ll win with speed to power. He’s a physical presence along the defensive front, particularly on third-down packages, and it’s been fun to watch him settle in. This was the best week of practice he’s had as a Lion, with a couple of sacks and a handful of pressures when given chances to rush. He’s ready for his close-up.
“It can help me a lot, just getting back into the rhythm,” Moore said of playing in the preseason. “I’ve been out for two weeks, so getting back into the rhythm, being able to go against different competitions and seeing different looks and different things like that, and just showing everybody what I’m capable of doing.”
Campbell and special teams coordinator Dave Fipp have raved about Martin and his contributions. He seems to have left his mark on special teams. When you’re talking about players fighting for a roster spot, that’s what it typically comes down to.
“Tay Martin’s jumped off the film every day,” Fipp said this week.
“Special teams is going to have a huge factor,” Campbell said. “… Tay Martin, man, makes plays every day. And he’s intriguing on offense, but he makes special teams plays every day. And that’s important to us.”
Chances are, the Lions likely won’t need Martin much on offense. It’s rare to be down to your No. 6 receiver. Instead, those guys make the roster because of what Martin has already proved capable of doing — adding value on special teams. The most important step is complete. That said, if Martin can add a cherry on top as a receiver in these final two preseason games, he’ll make this an easy decision for Campbell and general manager Brad Holmes.
The recent injury to Lions tight end Sam LaPorta could have a trickle-down effect on roster construction if he’s unable to play in the season opener. LaPorta, dealing with a hip injury after taking a hit in Monday’s practice, is likely to be shelved for the foreseeable future. The Lions will take things slow with their star tight end, hoping rest will help him get ready for Week 1. But if it’s looking as if LaPorta will need more time, could the Lions roster four tight ends to begin the season? If that’s the case, you have to think they’d be looking for more of a receiving tight end, which could pave the way for Meeks to make a push.
Meeks caught a touchdown in Thursday’s practice and caught one pass for 17 yards in the preseason opener. The Lions began the process of converting Meeks, a former wide receiver, to tight end during the 2025 season. This is his first full season as a tight end, and we’ve seen him with his hands in the dirt blocking quite a bit. He’s not a finished product, but the Lions might have something with Meeks if they continue developing him. And they might need him if LaPorta isn’t ready.
“We like him and really felt like this is probably — this would give him the best shot to make our roster and help us,” Campbell said of moving Meeks to TE. “He brings a different flavor to the tight end room. He’s a big — call it big skill. He’s a big skill player. Because now some of those things that were out there at receiver, the X receiver, but all of a sudden you move him back inside, and now, man, the athleticism goes way up, right? And the speed and the ability to separate, catch the football, it really has shown moving him to the tight end position. And I really felt like that’s where we needed to see the most. And then the other (stuff) will come, like the run game, the blocking. He’s strong, he’s tough, he’s willing. So, as long as you have that, I don’t care if you’re 220, you’ll be just fine. We can use you in a role.”
You’ll often see the coaching staff reward young players for catching their eye with added snaps with a first-team unit. It’s the ultimate sign of growth for this coaching staff. One player whose growth has been linear this camp is Abney.
A player widely viewed as a Day 2 pick, Abney fell to the fifth round in April’s draft. You can come up with different reasons why. His lack of size and elite speed, his aggressive play style, you name it. But Abney’s instincts and fearless makeup were always going to leave an impact on this staff. It’s what they covet from their defensive backs, and it felt like only a matter of time until he was put to the test.
Abney showed his physical presence in the Lions’ preseason opener. In practice since, he has been worked in with the first-team defense at nickel and even locked up Amon-Ra St. Brown on a rep. Though youth might keep him from winning the job at this point, he’s firmly in the mix as this competition unfolds. It’ll likely come down to Abney, Christian Izien, Roger McCreary and perhaps Rakestraw (if healthy) for the starting nickel position. We’ll see if he can separate from the pack.

full_text:
Travis Hunter, who added 10-12 pounds of muscle this offseason, should benefit from a defensive scheme in Jacksonville. Ella Hall / Associated Press
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — The Jacksonville Jaguars’ most electrifying playmaker had very little to do with their historic turnaround in 2025.
So, in some ways, two-way star Travis Hunter’s sophomore season should carry even more hype — not less — than his disproportionately anticipated rookie season, which was cut short in a Week 9 practice when he tore the LCL in his right knee. The Jaguars traded an extra first-round pick to move up to No. 2 in the 2025 NFL Draft to select Hunter, but they didn’t get much bang for their buck. Hunter finished his rookie campaign with only 28 catches, 298 yards and one touchdown on offense, with three pass breakups and 15 total tackles on defense. He played an average of 69 snaps over seven games, 46 on offense and 23 on defense.
It’s understandable why Hunter is no longer the one-man thrill ride everyone wants to talk about as he was a summer ago; the Jaguars and their opponents alike were fascinated by his combination of talent and utilization. However extreme, he was billed as football’s answer to Shohei Ohtani, yet Hunter closed the season as an afterthought.
This year, the Jaguars are not eager to put too much pressure on Hunter and are happy to let him fly under the radar a little bit.
“We’re really looking forward to seeing him just go play ball and let him do his thing,” Jaguars coach Liam Coen told The Athletic recently.
Coen, the first rookie coach in history to lead a team from four wins to 13, has even adjusted Hunter’s plan. The Jaguars expect Hunter to play more cornerback than receiver this season, which they say is more of a nod to their depth chart than his skill set or development.
To their point, the Jaguars need significantly more from their cornerbacks this season. Last year, they flipped Tyson Campbell for Greg Newsome in an attempt to find a better scheme fit, but Newsome struggled in the playoff loss to the Buffalo Bills before departing in free agency. This season, the Jags hope Hunter and Montaric “Buster” Brown can better solidify the position.
The positional deployment might benefit Hunter, too. Before being drafted, teams generally believed Hunter was better suited to be a full-time corner and part-time wideout in the NFL, though the Jags saw it the other way. They wanted him to gain as much experience as possible in Coen’s offense while mixing in at corner.
Now, Hunter is preparing to serve as the team’s No. 1 cornerback. Defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile’s zone-based system will likely keep Hunter to a side of the field rather than a receiver-based assignment, at least for a majority of the time.
Hunter, who has added 10-12 pounds of muscle this offseason, will also greatly benefit from facing the line of scrimmage and attacking the ball with anticipation, which is one of his greatest strengths. That also aligns with Campanile’s schematic vision, as he took over a unit that ranked last with nine turnovers in 2024 and led them to 31 takeaways in 2025, second most in the league.
Another boost: Coen ordered the construction of a virtual meeting room over the offseason, knocking down a wall and installing top-of-the-line software to aid the team’s mental reps. According to those around the Jaguars, Hunter has utilized the room more than anyone, and it’s not particularly close. He can walk into the room, listen to the defensive play call, move to his spot within the formation, watch the offense virtually line up and then handle the necessary checks and communication assignments from there.
“He’s done so much work in the virtual meeting rooms, walkthroughs, (traditional) meeting room,” Coen said. “That’s been a huge part of his growth and maturation throughout this training camp. He’s put in a lot of time and built his body back up in a physical way, especially his upper half. Just getting him playing confident, to really go out and play. He hasn’t played football in a long time, so we’re really in that ramp-up process.”
To be fair, there were concerns about Hunter’s durability before he entered the league, strictly out of skepticism that a two-way player could hold up with a significant jump in physicality from the University of Colorado to the NFL. It’d be unfair to connect those concerns with the knee injury, but it will be important for Hunter to get through a full season to alleviate any lingering doubts. The mental reset and added mass should conceivably help.
Offensively, the Jaguars are preparing to pick Hunter’s spots. Aside from plays specifically designed around him, look for Hunter to draw much of his early work in crucial situations, including money downs and in the red zone. But they’re also getting Hunter ready to take on an expanded role in case Jakobi Meyers, Parker Washington or Brian Thomas Jr. go down with injuries.
There will also be games when the matchup calls for a more offensive tilt, so of course, the Jaguars have a generalized plan for Hunter’s usage. But they aren’t trying to pigeonhole him.
The Jaguars’ ultimate goal is the same with Hunter; the path to it just might look a bit different this year. And for an organization that is trying to secure back-to-back playoff appearances for the first time since the 1990s, Hunter’s newish look should be a boon in Jacksonville.
“We expect him,” Coen said, “to really have a huge impact for our team.”

full_text:
Patrick Mahomes' recovery from knee surgery and the emergence of rookies, including receiver Cyrus Allen, right, were among the biggest storylines during Chiefs training camp. Denny Medley / Imagn Images
ST. JOSEPH, Mo. — The Kansas City Chiefs wrapped up 18 days of full-squad training camp on Missouri Western’s campus Thursday.
Here are six things we learned about the roster over the last three weeks:
Thanks to strenuous offseason knee rehab — and with help from motivating texts from NFL tight end Zach Ertz — quarterback Patrick Mahomes was cleared fully to participate at the start of training camp.
Since then, it’s been difficult to tell he’s only eight months post-surgery. Mahomes went through rollouts, scrambled when needed and even did some of his patented off-balance, twisting throws in drills, making it all but certain he’ll be the Chiefs’ starting quarterback in the season opener against the Denver Broncos.
Will he be limited a bit physically? Sure. Those coming off a torn ACL/LCL typically require more than a year to be fully back, and Mahomes acknowledged this setback might be something he’ll be adjusting to the rest of his career.
The most important thing so far, though, is Mahomes still looks like himself. In recent weeks especially, the knee and brace he wears haven’t seemed to come to his mind during the most competitive moments, suggesting he’s cleared a significant mental hurdle there.
The Chiefs have loved what they’ve gotten out of free agent Kenneth Walker III, as a complete running back and off-field leader.
It’s led to one of the most striking parts of training camp: They are getting the ball to Walker all the time .
This wasn’t the case for most of his Seattle Seahawks tenure. Walker shared the backfield with Zach Charbonnet, which meant mostly early down work.
That won’t be the case with the Chiefs. Coach Andy Reid opened up his screen-game playbook this summer, and Walker has been the primary target, showing strong receiving skills while even flashing occasional one-handed catches.
Then in the red zone? Walker has been the main guy again, meaning he should easily eclipse last year’s five-touchdown total if he remains healthy this season.
Though the Chiefs often have alternated backs by series in past seasons, that doesn’t appear to be the plan in 2026. Walker should be the workhorse, and he’s primed for a huge year statistically if his body holds up.
You shouldn’t sign Walker if you don’t plan to run the ball more, and the Chiefs have shown a concerted effort in training camp to be more of the downhill team that general manager Brett Veach envisioned back at the NFL combine.
Reid has unquestionably run more under-center plays this camp than in any of the last few seasons. Defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo mentioned last week that his defense was seeing a lot more run plays from the offense this summer, and linebacker Nick Bolton reiterated that sentiment Thursday.
“They did a great job,” Bolton said of the offense in practice, “of mixing the run, pass, play-actions.”
Reid commented at the end of last year that the team’s lack of an explosive run game hampered its play-action ability. In short, opposing linebackers weren’t coming upfield on run fakes, which made it difficult to create passing lanes in the second level of the defense.
Defenses will have to respect Walker, though. That was evident on Walker’s only play of the preseason opener, when Los Angeles Rams linebacker Daniel Rickert bit hard on a run fake that opened up the middle of the field.
Reid has faced some questions this offseason, about his offense and his ability to adapt in the modern NFL. Early indications, however, are that the Chiefs spent the offseason examining their flaws and making notable schematic changes as they look to bounce back from a 6-11 season.
While most of the offseason talk has centered on the Chiefs’ lack of perceived depth at wide receiver, a different position group appears to be the bigger red flag right now: interior offensive line.
The Chiefs have signaled this with their actions when a few guys have been held out of practices because of injuries. Veteran Jaylon Moore and undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson have been competing for the starting right tackle job, but it’s been telling that both have been shuffled to right guard during recent drills — an indication coaches see them as more capable backups inside than roster vets like Mike Caliendo and Hunter Nourzad.
Right guard Trey Smith has missed over a week of practices with a back injury, but the good news for the Chiefs is it’s not considered severe and he’s expected back soon. The fact that an injury to any guard or tackle could put the team into immediate scramble mode, though, is not ideal.
Don’t be surprised if the Chiefs look to upgrade this spot over the next few weeks.
Reid, a man who typically withholds praise unless someone truly earns it, mentioned Thursday that one of his biggest takeaways from training camp was the growth of the rookies.
“I think we made progress. I think it’s the young guys that you’re really looking at,” Reid said. “We have a number of them, and how they progressed — and continue to progress — will be a big part of how this team does.”
Chiefs rookie stocks certainly have been up in recent days.
No. 6 pick Mansoor Delane is the wild card after missing a lot of on-field reps because of a shoulder injury. Spagnuolo sees those experiences as extremely valuable, so it’s a bit concerning that Delane has been a full-go with the team only over the last week.
Still, Delane has come back with confidence. He’s played with physicality and swagger, to the point that the Chiefs might have to ask him to back off a bit on his technique so his “handsiness” doesn’t result in flags early this season.
Outside of Delane, there should be a lot of reason for rookie optimism. Some highlights:
• First-round defensive tackle Peter Woods flashed early with his speed and quick hands, even if an ankle injury has limited some burst over the last week;
• Fifth-round receiver Cyrus Allen was an early camp standout and appears to be gaining Mahomes’ trust;
• Fifth-round running back Emmett Johnson impressed during the preseason opener , and his ability to take on tough coaching from offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy and running backs coach DeMarco Murray has only helped accelerate his development;
• Benson — after getting signed as a tryout player from rookie minicamp — is pushing to be the starter at right tackle and, at worst, will be valuable offensive line depth on a team that needs it.
The Chiefs appeared to need an infusion of youth and speed after last year’s disappointing season, and early returns are positive for some of the newbies looking to step into important roles.
The Chiefs looked to model some of the other top NFL defenses this offseason while compiling a rotation of bodies they could use on the defensive line.
Veach, to this point, has to be pleased with how that revamp looks.
All-Pro defensive tackle Chris Jones returns as an anchor, but he should have much more help this season. Veteran free agent Khyiris Tonga has had competitive one-on-one battles with four-time Pro Bowl center Creed Humphrey in practice — a rare sight in camp that should indicate the floor has been raised with his addition.
Edge rusher George Karlaftis, meanwhile, is healthy again after playing with a broken hand last season. Woods has provided juice on the interior in practices, and second-round rookie R Mason Thomas shot around the edge for a pair of pressures in the preseason opener that looked like a different speed from edge rushers of the past.
Chiefs 2025 second-round defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott should return at some point after an ACL injury, and 2023 first-round pick Felix Anudike-Uzomah has flashed with his best camp as a pro. Ashton Gillotte (foot) is injured with an uncertain timeline at this point, but he joins veteran Emmanuel Ogbah in a group that has both potential…

title: Eagles-Patriots observations: Jalen Hurts' clutch TD drive, skirmishes stall running game Hurts and A.J. Brown, who had not spoken since Brown was traded to the Patriots in June, embraced after Thursday's joint practice. Zach Berman
summary:

FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — If the last impression is the lasting impression, then the Philadelphia Eagles should leave encouraged by their offense in Thursday’s joint practice against the New England Patriots. For much of the session, the offense would not deserve the same praise. There were interceptions, incompletions and a few tussles from cranky
full_text:
Jalen Hurts and the Eagles ended joint practices with the Patriots Thursday, and the teams will play a preseason game Saturday. Billie Weiss / Getty Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — If the last impression is the lasting impression, then the Philadelphia Eagles should leave encouraged by their offense in Thursday’s joint practice against the New England Patriots. For much of the session, the offense would not deserve the same praise. There were interceptions, incompletions and a few tussles from cranky and competitive players on a hot and humid New England morning. Then, during the final period for full-team, competitive drills, Jalen Hurts led the Eagles on a touchdown drive with clutch passes for an emphatic finish to two days of work against the defending AFC champions.
And yes, he even caught up with an old friend. Here’s what mattered from the offense Thursday:
1. Makai Lemon returned to practice on a limited basis for the first time in nearly three weeks. This was major news for the Eagles and a positive sign for the offense, giving Lemon three full weeks of practice ahead of the season opener. Lemon is expected to have a major role in the passing game and had been working as one of the top three receivers in the offense with DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks before his injury on Aug. 3. He also missed most of the spring.
Makai Lemon getting some work in near the end zone pic.twitter.com/FwZnwcwI2r
— Brooks Kubena (@BKubena) August 20, 2026
Lemon and Smith did not participate in team drills, so the Eagles did not showcase the complete offense this week. The key is that Lemon’s injury will not stretch into the season. Nick Sirianni said Lemon could stay up to speed without the on-field work, too.
“The extra meeting time, being able to go through some of that stuff,” Sirianni said. “Even just in that time, too, you can walk through some things in the meeting room. Always mentally, you’re doing everything you can do to help that. And then obviously too, you want to be in great shape. There’s things that you can do there as well as far as what he’s doing in the training room to make sure that he’s in as good of shape as he possibly can be when he steps back out on the field. All those things are thought about, and we’re working through all those things right now.”
2. The best sequence came at the end of practice. It was the only period when both teams were on the same field, and it was a competitive, last-minute situation. The Patriots had the ball at their 25-yard line, and Jalyx Hunt made a diving interception on the first play to give Hurts and the offense the ball. One day earlier, the Eagles struggled in the hurry-up drill and could not score. That stung the offensive players after practice.
This time, they had a money drive. It started with a completion to Dallas Goedert, giving the offense momentum. A pass to Wicks followed. Hurts almost found Hollywood Brown for a touchdown, but Brown was out of bounds in the back of the end zone. No matter. He found Brown one play later for the score — and it was punctuated by a 2-point conversion to Darius Cooper. The passing game came alive in a critical situation and showed it could move the ball even without Smith and Lemon.
After practice, Goedert said the first completion is key in those situations. When Sean Mannion discusses staying on schedule, this is an example. The offense moved quickly; Hurts is dangerous near the end zone by moving the defense when he improvises, and the pass catchers made plays. It could look even better with Smith and Lemon. I don’t want to overstate one sequence, but it was an impressive way to finish practice.
Successful two days @Patriots 🤝 pic.twitter.com/Seqjk7gI0D
— Philadelphia Eagles (@Eagles) August 20, 2026
3. That last period overshadowed what had been an inconsistent day for the passing offense. Hurts threw two interceptions to Marcus Jones, including one on a deflected pass to Brown. He was also under duress from the Patriots’ pass rush, with multiple would-be sacks. The interceptions are uncustomary for Hurts but were more frequent this week. This offense will target the middle of the field, so there might be more “interceptable” passes this year. It’s a number worth monitoring for Hurts; he had 11 total interceptions over the last two seasons, down from 15 in 2023. His interception rate has been 1.4 percent or lower in three of the past four years.
There were some good moments, including two touchdowns in a red zone period (one to Goedert, one to Wicks), but it wasn’t as smooth a performance as you would like to see from the passing offense. It sounds repetitive, but I expect it to look more efficient when the top receivers return. Both Smith and Lemon can help with quick completions that move the chains.
4. It’s worth singling out Goedert. He had a good day (and has had a solid summer) and is especially effective in the red zone. Goedert tied for an NFL lead among tight ends with 11 touchdowns last season, and the 2025 offensive staff was creative in finding ways to get him the ball in the low red zone. It would make sense for Sean Mannion to do the same this year. This offense asks him to play differently, but it’s a scheme that can use a strong tight end because of all the condensed formations. Goedert must stay healthy (he played 15 games last year for the first time in four seasons); as long as he’s on the field, he’ll be one of Hurts’ top targets.
5. The running game was not as effective as it was one day earlier. It seemed stuck at times. Don’t take it from me. Take it from Jordan Mailata:
“Yesterday was a better day for us running the ball — (Thursday), not so good — but yesterday we were able to see with the misdirections and the way the concept is designed, the ball can hit anywhere,” Mailata said.
“The run game had a better flow yesterday,” Mailata said. “There were less fights. The fights, we’ve got to cut that out because it cuts momentum. Both sides are amped up, and we’re not thinking about our assignment, we’re thinking about roughing the next guy. Which is great, but not effective in our scheme and our concept of things. There were no fights yesterday. It was a pretty clean practice. We were able to build on that momentum — even if it was two yards, three yards, each yard kept leading to more yards. We weren’t effective (Thursday) because we decided to put the boxing gloves on (Thursday).”
6. There were certainly more skirmishes between the Eagles offense and Patriots defense. These weren’t full-fledged fights like Moro Ojomo vs. Fred Johnson last week, but this practice was more heated. (And in the heat, too; this one felt stickier than most sessions.) There were times when Saquon Barkley was thudded more than the Eagles linemen appreciated — there’s no tackling to the ground in these sessions — and the Eagles stood up for their running back. There was one instance when Wicks went after a Patriots defender and needed to be separated.
Barkley expressed his disdain for joint practices and said he prefers one day of them. By the second day, the novelty wears off, and the two teams can get irritated at each other. Mailata thought it took away from the quality of practice.
“Less boxing and more football,” Mailata said. “Just boys being boys. It’s football, you know? I think guys running in — myself included — made it worse. You can’t help but want to be there for your teammates. Each situation is different. Guys were running from all over the place (Thursday) to get a piece of the opposition. It starts with me, and I’ve got to be better with that. But we’ve got to remember when we start fights, we take away reps from the younger guys. It’s unfortunate.”
7. Two wrinkles in the offense on Thursday that stood out …

full_text:
Spencer Anderson has finally made a name for himself in Pittsburgh. Michael Owens / AP
The day after the Steelers selected Spencer Anderson, the 2023 seventh-round pick was instructed to call then-assistant offensive line coach Isaac Williams.
Hey coach, Spencer Anderson here.
Coach, this is Spencer Anderson.
“One more time for me,” Anderson remembers Williams saying.
Uhh you drafted me. Spencer Anderson.
That first conversation told the rookie plenty about what life is like as a late-round pick. The Steelers had made a splashy move that year when they traded up in the first round to draft offensive tackle Broderick Jones. Anderson waited until pick No. 251 — eight spots ahead of so-called Mr. Irrelevant, the NFL Draft’s final selection. Sometimes, Anderson felt like he should have the tongue-in-cheek tagline.
“I always felt like I was the middle child or the stepson, however you want to look at it,” Anderson said. “Nobody knew who I was and what I could do, to be honest.”
Now in his fourth NFL season, Anderson has worked himself into a position to change that. The 6-5, 305-pound lineman has been running with the first-team offense at right guard since OTAs. In one of the few position battles that’s not totally settled, Anderson will still need to hold off Brock Hoffman over the final two preseason games, including on Friday when the Steelers host the New York Jets. However, the once-forgotten seventh-round pick remains in pole position to start Week 1.
“Competition, it’s always a constant,” Anderson said. “Just proving myself right every day. This all comes down to me proving to myself that I belong here and I could fulfill my childhood dreams.”
While the opportunity to win a starting job out of camp is new, fighting for a roster spot is not. Players who join the Steelers in the seventh round aren’t guaranteed much more than a dorm room at Saint Vincent College and some cafeteria lunches. During Anderson’s first training camp in Latrobe, former head coach Mike Tomlin pulled Anderson aside and reminded him of this fact.
“He told me, ‘There’s no such thing as the third group in the NFL, so you better get going,'” Anderson said.
Translation: If you’re not a primary backup, you’re not making the team.
“That was all the motivation I needed,” Anderson said.
Under the previous regime, a sign hung over the door in the offensive line room that read, in part: “The day you put your hand in the dirt is the day you made a decision to toil away in anonymity.” Anderson, who recited the line unprompted, took it to heart.
“The best advice I ever got was from James Daniels and (Chukwuma Okorafor): Don’t get hurt,” Anderson said. “As much as I was hurting back when I was rookie, like Coach (Tomlin) said, ‘People either don’t care about your problems, or they’re glad you have them.'”
Versatility is where Anderson showed his value. He played all five offensive line positions at the University of Maryland. Early in his first training camp, the Steelers told Anderson his best shot of making the 53-man roster was as a tackle, a position he hadn’t played in three years. As his career unfolded, the Steelers continued to move Anderson where he was needed. Some reps at tackle. Some at center. Most of his starts came at guard when others sustained injuries that thrust Anderson into the starting role. Last year, former offensive coordinator Arthur Smith came up with yet another way to tap into Anderson’s versatility by deploying him as an extra lineman in jumbo packages .
“Being a late-round guy, you’ve got to find any way to try to make yourself as valuable as possible,” Anderson said. “Just doing as much as I could to make the team.”
This offseason, the Steelers overhauled their coaching staff in the wake of Tomlin’s resignation . When offensive line coach James Campen first spoke with Anderson, the conversation took on a much different tone. The last staff asked who he was; this one asked which position he prefers.
“Obviously, being a seventh-round pick, I never got to choose,” Anderson said. “If I had to choose, I’d say right (guard).”
The staff took input from all of the players and also factored in each lineman’s background. They ultimately decided to flip tackle Troy Fautanu and guard Mason McCormick to the left side, where they played extensively in college. With Isaac Seumalo departing in free agency, that opened a door for Anderson to step in as the starting right guard.
Holding on to the position could help set up Anderson for the next stage of his career. He has already seen the Steelers hand out big-money contracts to three members of his draft class: defensive lineman Keeanu Benton, tight end Darnell Washington and outside linebacker Nick Herbig. At the same time, the team has also begun preparing for the future in some ways, drafting Gennings Dunker in the third round.
If Anderson can hold his spot atop the depth chart, he won’t have to introduce himself to the team that decides to sign him to his next contract.

title: Who is Jack Pyburn and what would happen if the Buccaneers LB returns to college? Pyburn would have to repay his NFL signing bonus if he returned to college football, while the Buccaneers would retain his rights. Saad Yousuf 1
summary:
Jack Pyburn seemed to boost his NFL stock with his debut preseason performance, but will he return to college football instead? Margaret Bowles / Associated Press
After a strong performance in the preseason opener for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, it appeared undrafted rookie linebacker Jack Pyburn was setting himself up for an NFL future. Instead, Pyburn is one of 16 former college football players, some of whom are signed to NFL contracts, who are looking to return to college for the 2026 season.
full_text:
Jack Pyburn seemed to boost his NFL stock with his debut preseason performance, but will he return to college football instead? Margaret Bowles / Associated Press
After a strong performance in the preseason opener for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, it appeared undrafted rookie linebacker Jack Pyburn was setting himself up for an NFL future. Instead, Pyburn is one of 16 former college football players, some of whom are signed to NFL contracts, who are looking to return to college for the 2026 season.
This unprecedented situation of a player going from the NFL back to the NCAA stems from Louisiana’s 19th Judicial District Court granting a temporary restraining order that could allow more than 30 college athletes a fifth year of eligibility. Pyburn played his first three seasons of college football at the University of Florida before playing a fourth season at LSU in 2025. The TRO would not only allow Pyburn to return to college football, but he would be able to enter the transfer portal, where schools can bid for his services. He would be eligible for the upcoming college football season, which begins in a few weeks.
“I saw the ruling,” Buccaneers coach Todd Bowles said Thursday. “I have not heard anything from him.”
Pyburn was seen practicing with the team Thursday. Tampa Bay resumes its preseason schedule Saturday when it hosts the Kansas City Chiefs.
If Pyburn did go back to college, Tampa Bay would retain his NFL rights. According to the league’s collective bargaining agreement, “If Player … fails or refuses to perform his services under this contract, then this contract will be tolled between the date of Player’s … failure or refusal to perform, and the later date of his return to professional football.”
That means the three-year contract he signed with the Bucs would effectively pause and resume if and when he returned to the NFL.
The recent saga is just the latest in a long list of lawsuits regarding NCAA eligibility disputes. At the heart of the issue is the financial element, which was highlighted by another case earlier this offseason. Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss and his lawyers fought the NCAA to allow him to stay in college for another year, even though Chambliss was projected to be a mid-round draft pick. As The Athletic outlined in that situation , Chambliss is expected to make between $5 million and $6 million this season at Ole Miss. Even if Chambliss fell on the lower end of that spectrum, he will still make more than 246 of the 257 players drafted in the 2026 NFL Draft.
As an undrafted free agent this year, even if his training camp and preseason performance helps his case for an NFL roster spot, Pyburn’s financial upside for the 2026 season could be higher in the college ranks. Pyburn received a $15,000 signing bonus from the Buccaneers and was guaranteed $100,000 for the upcoming season. If he were to make an NFL team and spent the entire season on the 53-man roster, he’d make the league minimum of $885,000. A full season on an NFL practice squad would earn him about $250,000.
Given the nature of a player on an NFL contract returning to college, the TRO does outline that the player may go down that path “so long as they terminate any such contract and repay any money they have received prior to playing in a collegiate game.” That means Pyburn would have to pay back the signing bonus he received from the Bucs.
Pyburn was graded as a sixth-round pick in The Beast, with draft expert Dane Brugler evaluating him as a player who “doesn’t offer much upside as a pass rusher, but he is stout versus the run and competes with a touch of insanity to him (in a good way).” Brugler highlighted Pyburn’s 574 special-teams snaps in college as an asset that could result in him making “the back end of an NFL roster.”
Pyburn was spotlighted by The Athletic ’s Daniel Popper as one of 11 roster bubble players last week who stood out across the NFL after the first week of preseason, both for his sacks and his special-teams potential.
“Teams need their end-of-the-depth-chart edge rushers to play special teams,” Popper wrote. “Pyburn looks like he would be capable. But some NFL film in that phase could enhance how attractive he is on the waiver wire, if he makes it there.”
Bowles, speaking earlier this week about Pyburn’s preseason performance, also highlighted his special-teams skills.
“If you’re going to be toward the back end of the outside (linebackers), you’ve got to be able to play special teams, and you’ve kind of got to be a jack-of-all-trades and do certain things,” Bowles said. “He made us watch it. He made it known, and we’re going to see what he does going forward, but he definitely made an impression.”
Pyburn also spoke to reporters earlier in the week and was asked how he deals with the uncertainty of training camp.
“I’m not really worried about what the outcome is,” he said. “If anything, I’m just going to continue my daily process, and at the end of the day try to be the best player that I can be, and hopefully one day that’s one of the best in the league.”
— NFL writer Daniel Popper contributed to this report.

title: Latest Tip Reiman Injury Update Has Tough Decision Looming for Cardinals
full_text:
Soon, the Arizona Cardinals may be forced with a tough roster decision regarding tight end Tip Reiman.
The former third-round pick isn't going to be released or cut, though a severe ankle injury suffered in October of last season still lingers. While he's been spotted rehabbing off to the side of Cardinals practices, his placement on PUP at the beginning of training camp hasn't changed.
That doesn't appear to be the case anytime soon, as Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters Reiman likely isn't going to be ready for the regular season opener.
"No with Tip, but again he's progressing. There's just conversations [to be had]," LaFleur told reporters.
"Again, it's just day to day. He's putting in a ton of work as well, so that's just that's just day to day. He's a large man too, right? And putting a lot of force in that. There's the good days and there's the not as good days, but putting in a lot of work. We'll see."
That's a massive pivot from earlier in the offseason, when LaFleur said the Cardinals expected Reiman to be ready for training camp. Now, one of their best blockers is doubtful for the regular season opener and perhaps beyond.
The Cardinals have a massive decision coming on Reiman in terms of his status on the PUP list. If Reiman remains, he'll have to miss the first four games of the season.
"Those are the tough decisions, and you lean on the player to speak truth as well, and trust these guys," LaFleur said when asked if Reiman was going to stay on PUP.
"Tip is made of all the right stuff, so Tip's going to keep it real with us. But those are the decisions that have to be made for the reasons that you're saying."
Reiman figures to be a massive part of the Cardinals' efforts to establish the run.
"Another guy that I had a lot of respect for coming out of Illinois," LaFleur said earlier in the offseason.
"It's like some of those guys, when you get the job, you're like, 'Yes! I wanted him coming out of the draft!' and then you get to inherit him. I can say that easily about Tip because Tip is all of the right stuff in terms of how he approaches it and stuff like that. It was unfortunate what happened a year ago, but big piece of where I think we can go."

title: Garrett Williams' Return From Injury Gives Cardinals Boost at the Right Time
full_text:
ARIZONA — The return of Garrett Williams is here, and it couldn't have come at a better time.
The Arizona Cardinals activated Williams off the PUP list today as the slot cornerback is set to begin practicing for the first time in 2026 following an Achilles tear he suffered in late December of last year.
"We're going to take that one day at a time. The human element, a lot of work was put in first and foremost by him, and then a lot of people behind the scenes to get to this point," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters.
"So happy for him. He's had a smile on his face, we've known this day was coming for some time now, and it's time for the next step."
Williams' importance to the secondary can't be overstated. When healthy, he's one of the best slot cornerbacks in the league while his versatility to also play on the boundary and sometimes safety is often utilized under defensive coordinator Nick Rallis.
"It's really no different from a receiver that plays inside the numbers, inside the alleys, inside the paint. You got to be able to muck it up. You got to mix it up. You got to be physical. It's a different game than it used to be in there," LaFleur added.
"So he's got the size. He's got the want to. He's got the smarts. He's a good player, and we're excited to have him back."
Before injuries plagued Williams in 2025, he was graded among the best cornerbacks in Pro Football Focus' database — ranking behind just Trent McDuffie and Patrick Surtain entering the season.
"Definitely excited to get Garrett back," Cardinals captain Budda Baker said.
"He brings a lot of knowledge and always there in the right spot, always doing his job at a high level. Definitely special to get him back practicing with us. Of course, they'll take it easy on him, but definitely just to see him come back from that, it's definitely something very special. Just excited to have him doing our DB work and stuff like that."
Williams' arrival to the Cardinals secondary now will bump Sean Murphy-Bunting (who moved into the slot this spring) into backup duties for the spot while he'll occupy a boundary role opposite of fellow cornerback Will Johnson.
"We'll do what we see is necessary depending on where this thing kind of goes, but right now the plan is to play him inside," said LaFleur. "... He does some really good stuff on the inside. Not that he can't on the outside, but that's where we'll start."

title: Cardinals Reveal QB Plan vs. Cowboys With Carson Beck Decision Made
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are set to face the Dallas Cowboys in preseason action this weekend, marking their only home game of the exhibition slate.
Despite having an established starting quarterback in Jacoby Brissett, the Cardinals' quarterback position has seen plenty of intrigue through the offseason thanks to Brissett's contract holdout, the addition of free agent signing Gardner Minshew and rookie third-round pick Carson Beck looming in the mix.
Ahead of Saturday, Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur met with reporters and detailed the quarterback plan against Dallas.
Brissett will not play, according to LaFleur. Minshew will be starting the first half, if not the beginning of the third quarter. Beck "most likely" will not play on Saturday while Kedon Slovis is set to play clean-up.
Brissett has played in one preseason game, going 5/5 against the Raiders for 44 yards and one touchdown pass.
Brissett is the obvious starter, at least for the beginning of the season, after Arizona handed him $15 million in guaranteed money for the last year of his contract. The early indications from camp and the minor preseason stint we saw were strong, though he's still catching back up to the offense.
"I'm catching up," Brissett told reporters after missing OTAs, minicamp and the first days of training camp due to the holdout. "I feel like I have made leaps and bounds."
Minshew featured in the win over Las Vegas last weekend, competing 14 of 16 passes for 101 yards and two touchdowns against the Raiders.
Minshew, as of now, is listed as QB2 on the team's depth chart and likely would be the first man up if Brissett needs replaced during action. His willingness to extend plays and push the ball downfield makes for an exciting brand of football, though sometimes turnovers do come back to haunt him.
Beck played in the Hall of Fame Game, impressing the entire country on a national spotlight after going 15 of 19 for 188 yards and one touchdown against the Carolina Panthers.
The rookie suffered a ribs injury in Canton, however, and was a late scratch from preseason action in Las Vegas last week. After not throwing at all this week in preperation for Dallas, his absence was expected.
Slovis is the only Cardinals quarterback to have played in both preseason games so far. He's competed 16 of 19 passes for 181 yards and one passing touchdown in total.
Slovis is likely going to be pretty active in the final two games for the Cardinals, given he's not a starter and is likely going to be waived ahead of 53-man roster cuts. However, he's operated well within LaFleur's system and could be auditioning for a role elsewhere through the NFL.

Rams safety Quentin Lake: "One of the bigger s--- talkers in the NFL, and he's going to let you hear about it. Can block, run routes, is looking for blood on the sideline. Can go outside and catch a fade ball or a slant in the red zone.

Saints safety Jonas Sanker: He's a competitor. He's a dog.
Texans tight end Dalton Schultz: "Dude, he's a dog. It's really hard going against our defense. Like, I know it's a pain in the ass. He had like 12 for 100-something, two touchdowns, he was shredding them.

title: Cardinals Rookie Has Stunning Chance to Return to College Football
full_text:
ARIZONA — In an odd turn of events, the Arizona Cardinals have a rookie that might be heading back to school.
Safety Wydett Williams was one of many college football players who were granted a temporary restraining order to play one more season at the NCAA level.
Former Ole Miss starters Dae'Quan Wright, Zxavian Harris and Wydett Williams, all of whom signed with NFL teams this summer, are among a group of athletes who were granted a temporary restraining order Wednesday to return to college for one more season. https://t.co/c1oVqqt55o
According to ESPN, a total of 16 players were listed in the lawsuit. The NCAA could potentially appeal the decision.
"Those players have expressed an interest in being released from their NFL contracts, according to attorney Ryan Downton, and if their NFL teams release them by Sept. 1 they will be allowed to join a college roster under the restraining order," said ESPN in their story .
The NCAA recently reworked its eligibility rules to allow five seasons to be played in five years, as opposed to four seasons. The Division I board of directors opted to not include recent seniors — which Williams was part of.
"NCAA officials said they did not want a sudden influx of returning fifth-year players to take roster spots from incoming freshmen, many of whom had already signed on to play for their teams by the time the rule was changed," ESPN continued.
"That decision prompted the current wave of lawsuits that have come through state and federal courts. In several cases, judges have granted temporary restraining orders that allow athletes to compete in the upcoming season while their case is pending."
Williams, listed at 6-1 and 200 lbs on his scouting profile, began his college career at Delta State before transferring to Louisiana-Monroe (2024) and Ole Miss (2025) before going undrafted this past spring.
Williams is not currently projected to make the Cardinals' 53-man roster but could end up on a practice squad. After going undrafted, perhaps Williams feels like he could improve his game and change his fate by the 2027 NFL Draft.
If he does depart, Williams will likely transfer to a different school that failed to supplement their safety position through either recruiting or the transfer portal.
NFL rosters are due to be cut down from 90 to 53 on Sunday, Aug. 30. Players released are subject to waivers, where other teams can add them to their roster/practice squad.
With Budda Baker, Andrew Wingard, Dadrion Taylor-Demerson and Kitan Crawford already on the roster, the Cardinals' safety room is fairly full — which will likely see Williams off the team.
Williams has nine total tackles across Arizona's two preseason games.
